useCases.headline: The loops that run a company

developers.heroDescription: Agents, skills, tools, connectors, schedules — all just files in a repo. Edit them in your IDE, run them locally, ship to the cloud with one command. Open source, self-hostable, yours.
developers.agentBody: An agent is Markdown — a persona, its model, and its tools. Skills are folders it loads on demand. Edit them by hand, or describe what you want and let your coding agent write them.
developers.shipBody: kortix ship commits, pushes, builds the sandbox, and prompts for missing secrets. Triggers and channels go live immediately — no separate infrastructure to set up.
developers.fleetBody: Every session is its own VM on its own branch, booting the runtime and your repo. Spawn thousands in parallel with zero interference. A change request is the only way work reaches main, so everything is reviewable and reversible.
developers.runtimeBody: Sessions run on an open runtime. Bring your own keys — Anthropic, OpenAI, or local — or use Kortix compute. Nothing about the runtime is hidden.
developers.lifecycleDescription: Scaffold, ship, run, automate, connect, and review — one CLI does it all. The same binary is pre-authenticated inside every sandbox, so agents drive Kortix with the exact commands you use.
developers.scaleDescription: Every session runs in its own isolated sandbox — real, isolated compute — on its own Git branch off main. Start millions in parallel; nothing collides.
developers.connectorsDescription: Kortix connectors put 3,000+ apps — plus any MCP, OpenAPI, GraphQL, or raw HTTP endpoint — behind one Executor interface that your agents call like any other tool.
developers.codeDescription: Because everything is code in a repo, the system can read its own blueprint, extend itself, and stay healthy as it grows. It is 100% extensible, controllable, and self-hostable — nothing is a black box.

1.question: What is a snapshot?
1.answer: A snapshot is a machine that has already been set up: this project’s repository, its dependencies, and the Kortix tools, all installed ahead of time. Starting a session copies that prepared machine instead of installing everything from scratch, which is why a session is ready in seconds rather than minutes.

2.question: Why do new rows keep appearing?
2.answer: Kortix prepares a new machine whenever the recipe changes — a new sandbox template, an edited Dockerfile, or a merged change — and each attempt gets its own row. Older rows are kept as a record. They are history, not a list of things to deal with.

3.question: One of them failed. Is that a problem?
3.answer: Usually not. A failed attempt only matters while no working machine is left, and when that happens a banner appears at the top of this page with a Rebuild button. A failed row with no banner above it has already been replaced by one that worked.

aiModelUsage.content: Different AI models have different costs based on their capabilities and token usage. Credits are consumed for input tokens (your prompts and context), output tokens (Worker responses), and vary by model tier (Claude, GPT, etc.).

pricingModel.title: Pricing
pricingModel.description: Platform rates vary by service type
pricingModel.content: We apply a markup on top of provider costs to cover platform infrastructure, security, and ongoing development. AI models have a 20% markup, tool usage (web search, scraping, etc.) has a 50% markup, image search has a 100% markup, and if you use your own API key, a flat 10% platform fee applies instead.

gettingMoreCredits.title: Getting More Credits
gettingMoreCredits.description: There are several ways to obtain credits in Kortix:

monthlySubscription.title: Monthly Subscription Credits
monthlySubscription.description: Included with your paid plan and renewed automatically each month. These are expiring credits.

topUpCredits.title: Top-Up Credits
topUpCredits.description: Purchase additional credits when you need them. These are non-expiring and available to premium members.

promotionalGrants.title: Promotional & Event Grants
promotionalGrants.description: Bonus credits from special events, promotions, or referrals. These are non-expiring.

refunds.title: Refunds
refunds.description: Credits returned due to technical issues or failed tasks. These are non-expiring.

typesOfCredits.title: Types of Credits
typesOfCredits.description: Kortix uses two types of credits to give you flexibility in how you manage your usage:

expiringCredits.title: Expiring Credits
expiringCredits.content: These credits are included with your paid subscription and are renewed automatically each month on your subscription date. They expire at the end of each billing cycle and are always consumed first before any non-expiring credits.

nonExpiringCredits.title: Non-Expiring Credits
nonExpiringCredits.content: These credits never expire and carry over month to month. They include top-up purchases, refunds, and promotional grants. Non-expiring credits are only used after your expiring credits have been depleted.

creditPriority.title: Credit Priority:
creditPriority.description: When you use Kortix, expiring credits are consumed first. Only after your expiring credits run out will non-expiring credits be used.

hub.faqBugQuestion: How do I request a feature or report a bug?
hub.faqBugAnswerAfter: with details. For bugs, include steps to reproduce and any error messages. Screenshots help.
hub.faqCreditsQuestion: What if I don't get credits after paying?
hub.faqCreditsAnswerAfter: immediately. We prioritize billing issues and typically resolve them within a few hours.
hub.faqConnectQuestion: Can Kortix connect to my apps?
hub.faqConnectAnswer: Yes. 3,000+ connectors via OAuth, MCP servers, REST APIs, CLI tools, and environment variables. If it has an interface, Kortix connects to it.
hub.faqWhatAnswer: A 24/7 cloud computer where AI agents do the actual work of running a company. You connect your tools, define your agents, set their schedules and triggers — and the machine operates whether you're there or not.
hub.faqDifferentQuestion: How is Kortix different from other AI platforms?
hub.faqDifferentAnswer: Most AI platforms are chat interfaces that give you suggestions. Kortix is a persistent computer that runs agents autonomously — they browse the web, execute code, call APIs, manage files, and coordinate across your tools. They work while you sleep.

appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line69JsxTextNotToolsNotAgentsNotWorkflo: Not tools. Not agents. Not workflows. Companies — with engineering departments, operations teams, finance functions, customer support, growth engines — that run themselves. Agents doing the actual work, 24/7, without a human touching every task.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line93JsxTextThisIsNotAForecastItIsOur: This is not a forecast. It is our operating target — the ratio we run ourselves at today, and the ratio we build toward with every company we work with. Humans are not removed. They are elevated. They set direction, review outputs, make final calls on things that matter. Agents handle the rest.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line111JsxTextAFactoryIsASystemForTurnin: A factory is a system for turning inputs into outputs at scale, reliably, repeatedly, without depending on any individual person being present. That is what we build for companies.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line118JsxTextYouFeedTheFactoryYourGoals: You feed the factory your goals, your tools, your context, your standards. The factory produces: shipped code, closed tickets, drafted contracts, reconciled books, outbound campaigns, synthesized research, recruited candidates. Every day. Whether you are in the office or asleep.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line138JsxAttrBodyEveryCompanyHasProcess: Every company has processes that run on human attention. We find them — support queues, reporting cycles, outbound sequences, QA checks, code review, invoice processing — and make them legible. You cannot automate what you have not named.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line143JsxAttrBodyEachProcessBecomesAnAg: Each process becomes an agent. Not a chatbot. Not a prompt wrapper. A specialist — with its own identity, permissions, tools, memory, and trigger rules. An engineering agent that ships PRs. A finance agent that closes the books. A support agent that resolves tickets before a human sees them.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line148JsxAttrBodyAgentsAreOnlyAsPowerfu: Agents are only as powerful as the tools they can reach. We wire the entire company stack — codebases, CRMs, databases, communication platforms, file systems, external APIs. An agent that cannot act is just a language model. An agent that can reach everything is an employee.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line153JsxTextGoalLoopTheAutonomousExecu: Goal loop: the autonomous execution loop. An agent takes a task, works it through to completion, self-verifies the result, and only stops when it can prove the output is correct. No hand-holding. No approval at every step. The job either gets done or the agent escalates with a clear explanation of why.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line158JsxAttrBodyEverySessionEveryDecis: Every session, every decision, every correction is retained. Agents remember what worked. They remember your preferences, your standards, your edge cases. The longer the factory runs, the smarter it gets. This is the compounding advantage humans cannot replicate at scale.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line163JsxAttrBodyTheFinalLayerIsHumanGo: The final layer is human governance: reviewing what matters, correcting course, setting new objectives. Not touching every task. Not approving every output. Governing the system. This is the 24% — and it is the most leveraged 24% these people will ever spend.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line178JsxTextWeRunOurOwnCompanyOnKortix: We run our own company on Kortix. Every day. Our engineering, our operations, our growth — agents doing the work, humans governing the system. We eat our own output before we ship it to anyone else.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line186JsxTextThisIsNotAProductDemoItIs: This is not a product demo. It is how we operate. The credibility of the playbook comes from the fact that we are living inside it. Every failure we encounter, we fix. Every edge case we hit, we document. The factory improves itself.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line203JsxTextKortixIsInfrastructureTheP: Kortix is infrastructure. The platform is not the point.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line209JsxTextThePointIsTheMigrationFrom: The point is the migration — from human-operated to AI-operated. From companies that require constant human attention to keep running, to companies that run themselves and only require human judgment to keep improving.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line217JsxTextWeThinkEverySeriousCompany: We think every serious company will make this migration in the next few years. The ones that move early will be operating at a cost base and execution speed that latecomers cannot catch. We are building the path — and walking it first.
appHomeFactoryFactoryClient.line228JsxTextWeAreASmallTeamWeCareThat: We are a small team. We care that the playbook is real, that it works, and that every company we help run this way comes out the other side faster and leaner than when they started.

appHomePage.differentScreenSectionDescription: Your team talks to agents from a clean web and mobile workspace, from Slack or Microsoft Teams, or right inside your own app via the API. Same agents, same guardrails, every surface.
appHomePage.companyAsCodeDescription: Every agent, skill, automation, and policy is a versioned file in a git repo you control. Diff it, review it, roll it back — like software. Run it on our cloud or self-host anywhere. No black box, no lock-in.
appHomePage.companyAsCodeBulletConfig: Agents, skills, and automations as plain files
appHomePage.companyAsCodeBulletGit: One config, one source of truth per company
appHomePage.companyAsCodeBulletSelfHost: Self-host on your cloud, VPC, or on-prem
appHomePage.connectorsTitle: One secure connection to every tool you run on.
appHomePage.connectorsDescription: 1-click connect to 3,000+ apps, plus any MCP, OpenAPI, or HTTP service. Agents get scoped, audited access through a single secure gateway — one connection, not fifty loose API keys.
appHomePage.connectorsBulletTwo: Bring any MCP, OpenAPI, or HTTP tool
appHomePage.connectorsBulletThree: Scoped per person, per agent, per team
appHomePage.connectorsBulletFour: Secrets stay encrypted and never leak into a session
appHomePage.enterpriseTitle: Built to survive a security review.
appHomePage.enterpriseDescription: Isolated execution, scoped credentials, a complete audit trail, and human approval gates — not retrofits, it's how Kortix is built. Run it on our cloud or your own infrastructure.
appHomePage.enterpriseScopedDescription: Per-resource permissions for every person and agent. SSO, RBAC, and groups.
appHomePage.enterpriseApprovalsDescription: Agents pause for sign-off before they touch anything that matters.
appHomePage.enterpriseIsolationDescription: Every session runs in its own sandboxed machine — MicroVM-level isolation.
appHomePage.enterpriseDataDescription: Self-host, VPC, on-prem, or air-gapped. Your data, config, and models stay yours.
appHomePage.enterpriseAccordionIsolationTeaser: One task, one workspace, one reviewable trail
appHomePage.enterpriseAccordionIsolationBody: Every session spins up its own isolated sandbox on its own Git branch — a clean clone of main with its own compute. Thousands of coworkers can run in parallel with zero crossover, and durable changes return only as reviewable change requests.
appHomePage.enterpriseAccordionTokenBody: Your API keys never enter a sandbox. Coworkers act through a single scoped Kortix token — permissions set per agent and per tool, network rules you control with allow, ask first, or block. Rotate one credential to revoke everything, everywhere.
appHomePage.enterpriseAccordionAuditTeaser: Logs, budgets, and a Git history
appHomePage.enterpriseAccordionAuditBody: Every model call passes through the LLM gateway with full logs, cost tracking, and per-team budgets. Every change — human or agent — lands as a Git commit you can review, diff, and revert. The audit trail isn't a feature bolted on; it's the repo itself.
appHomePage.enterpriseAccordionSocBody: Our SOC 2 Type II audit is underway. The controls it measures — isolated execution, scoped credentials, complete audit trails, access management — are already how Kortix is built, not retrofits. Security review documentation available on request.
appHomePage.enterpriseAccordionSelfhostBody: kortix self-host init runs the entire platform from Docker images — managed cloud, your VPC, on-prem, even air-gapped. Same product everywhere, nothing phones home. Your data, your models, your keys, on infrastructure you control.

appHomePage.workforceMapAutomationsDesc: Run on cloud, self-host, or VPC.

appHomePage.howItWorksSectionTitle: From a request to finished work.
appHomePage.howItWorksSectionDescription: Connect your tools, ask for the outcome, and review what comes back. The best workflows become reusable skills, and the company's memory compounds — for everyone.
appHomePage.storySkillsTitle: Turn your best workflows into skills everyone can use.
appHomePage.storySkillsDescription: Skills teach Kortix how your company does specific work: prepping for a sales call, triaging tickets, drafting a board update, reviewing contracts, or creating a campaign report.
appHomePage.storySkillsBulletCapture: Capture how your best people work
appHomePage.storySkillsBulletReuse: Reuse workflows across teams and agents
appHomePage.storySkillsBulletReview: Review and improve skills over time
appHomePage.storySkillsBulletDescription: Package the workflow once, improve it like a living playbook, and make it available to every coworker that needs it.
appHomePage.storyMemoryDescription: Kortix builds context from your connected tools, projects, files, previous work, and team knowledge. Every session starts with the background a capable coworker would already know.
appHomePage.storyMemoryBulletGrounded: Keeps output grounded in real tools and files
appHomePage.storyMemoryBulletDescription: The coworker starts with the context it needs, so the result gets sharper without another setup meeting.
appHomePage.storySurfacesTitle: You don't come to Kortix. It comes to you.
appHomePage.storySurfacesDescription: The friction of opening one more app is why most AI never gets used. So everyone uses the same agents, skills, and memory the easiest way — from Slack, Teams, the web, or their phone. Same config, same guardrails, every surface.
appHomePage.storySurfaceSlackBody: Turn channel requests into briefs, reports, and approvals — right in the thread.
appHomePage.storySurfaceSlackAsk: @Kortix pull last week's revenue and post it here
appHomePage.storySurfaceSlackReply: Revenue last week: $48.2k, up 12% week over week. Full breakdown attached.
appHomePage.storySurfaceTeamsBody: Bring Kortix into Teams so work moves where your projects already live.
appHomePage.storySurfaceTeamsAsk: @Kortix draft the QBR deck for Acme and tag me when it's ready
appHomePage.storySurfaceTeamsReply: Draft ready — 14 slides covering pipeline, churn, and Q3 targets. Tagging you for review.
appHomePage.storyOutcomesTitle: Start with one useful agent. Own the system it grows into.
appHomePage.storyOutcomesDescription: Pick one job that bounces between people, tabs, and tools, and hand it to an agent. It returns finished work — and becomes the first skill in a company that compounds.
appHomePage.storyUseCasesTitle: Start where work is already waiting.
appHomePage.storyUseCasesDescription: Kortix can help every team with the tools they already use. Pick a workflow, connect the right apps through Pipedream, and show a finished result people can review, send, or build on.
appHomePage.storyUseCasesGrowthSummary: For sales and marketing teams, Kortix handles the prep, cleanup, routing, and reporting that usually sits between meetings, CRM updates, spreadsheets, and Slack threads.
appHomePage.storyUseCasesPeopleLegalSummary: For people and legal teams, Kortix turns sensitive review work into a clear draft, scorecard, memo, or checklist with a human checkpoint before anything moves forward.
appHomePage.storyUseCasesFinanceOpsSummary: For finance and operations teams, Kortix helps with recurring close, cash, invoice, and leadership reporting work so teams spend less time assembling the same updates by hand.
appHomePage.storyUseCasesSupportDataSummary: For support and data teams, Kortix triages high-volume requests, turns resolved work into shared knowledge, and answers business questions from systems of record.

appHomePage.storyAlwaysOnDescription: Triggers fire on a schedule and on webhooks — overnight, on every event — so work is done before you ask. Agents can even propose changes to their own config, so the company files patches against itself and gets better at being a company over time.
appHomePage.storyOwnershipTitle: Own the AI system your company runs on.
appHomePage.storyOwnershipDescription: Kortix is open source and self-hostable. Run it on managed cloud, your VPC, on-prem, or air-gapped. Your data, tools, models, skills, and workflows stay under your control.
appHomePage.storyOwnershipNoLockIn: No black box or forced lock-in
appHomePage.forDevelopersPanelTitle: Built on files you can actually open.
appHomePage.forDevelopersPanelDescription: No SDK to learn, no API maze. Your agents, skills, and tools are plain files in a folder — clone the project, change what you want in your own editor, and ship it back.

i18nComplete.text7b84ea95f8ae: What does an agent actually run on?
i18nComplete.text97bbd1c3b346: Its own machine. Every session boots an isolated Linux cloud computer with your repo and your tools already on it, on its own git branch — the session id, the sandbox id and the branch name are one and the same string. The agent can install, run and break anything inside it; only what it commits survives, because the machine is destroyed with everything on it.
i18nComplete.textc145665dd580: What stops it doing something I did not want?
i18nComplete.texta9fe46474f33: You set allow, ask or block per action, and a rule can match on a glob, a regular expression, or the arguments of the call itself. Be aware that nothing is switched on for you: a project with no policy declared runs every action, so this is a thing you configure rather than a thing you inherit. Session work reaches main through a change request, and merge is default-deny for an agent — an admin has to grant it in kortix.yaml, and that grant is itself an edit somebody else has to merge.
i18nComplete.text3a8d0e57770e: Can I see everything an agent did?
i18nComplete.text36814e8d3c88: It is all recorded, on every plan. Recording is never gated — actions, approvals and the session transcript are captured whatever you pay. Reading, exporting and streaming that audit trail out to your own SIEM is an Enterprise entitlement, so on the lower plans the record exists but the export does not.
i18nComplete.textda09b5e9847d: No. A project is a git repository — clone it and the agents, the skills and everything the company has learned come with you. Self-host and the database, the files, the repos, the secrets and the audit record all sit on disk you control, on one Docker Compose stack built from the same images the managed cloud runs. It is not air-gapped, and we will not pretend otherwise: agent sandboxes run on the compute provider you configure, and your instance has to be reachable so they can call back.
i18nComplete.text151863950f0e: Can I use the models I already pay for?

The model is a line of configuration in your repo, so switching provider is a diff rather than a migration.

commandPalette.title: Command Palette
commandPalette.description: Search for a command to run...

company-memory.label: Onboard your agent
company-memory.prompt: Onboard me. Ask about my company — what we do, who our customers are, who's on the team, our products, our top priorities. Save what you learn into project memory so you remember it in every future session, and open a change request when you're done so I can review.

agent-create.label: Create an agent
agent-create.prompt: Create a specialist agent for a job my company does often. Write its prompt into `.kortix/opencode/agents/`, give it only the grants it actually needs in `kortix.yaml`, and open a change request so I can read it before it goes live. Pick the job that would save me the most time and tell me why you picked it.

agent-team.label: Build me a team of agents
agent-team.prompt: Design a small team of agents for my company — three or four specialists, each with a narrow job and a narrow grant — and explain how they hand work to each other. Write them up and open one change request with the lot.

skill-write.label: Write a skill
skill-write.prompt: Turn something my company does the same way every time into a skill under `.kortix/opencode/skills/`, so every future session already knows how. Pick the highest-value one, write it properly with the steps and the gotchas, and open a change request.

skill-from-runbook.label: Turn a habit into a skill
skill-from-runbook.prompt: I keep explaining the same process to you. Write it down as a reusable skill with the steps, the inputs, and what good output looks like, then open a change request. Ask me which process in one line if you cannot tell from memory.

agent-review.label: Review my agents
agent-review.prompt: Read every agent in this project — its prompt and its grants — and tell me which ones are vague, which are over-permissioned, and which overlap. Propose the fixes as one change request.

grants-audit.label: Audit what agents can reach
grants-audit.prompt: Audit `kortix.yaml`: for each agent, list the connectors, secrets and skills it can reach, and flag anything granted `all` that does not need it. Propose a tighter set as a change request.

trigger-daily.label: Schedule a daily briefing
trigger-daily.prompt: Set up a cron trigger that runs every weekday morning, gathers what changed in this project, and writes me a short briefing. Add it to `kortix.yaml`, keep it disabled, and tell me the one line to flip when I want it on.

trigger-weekly.label: Schedule a weekly report
trigger-weekly.prompt: Set up a weekly cron trigger that produces the report I would otherwise write by hand on Friday. Add it to `kortix.yaml` disabled, and show me exactly what it would have produced this week.

trigger-webhook.label: Fire work from a webhook
trigger-webhook.prompt: Set up a signed webhook trigger so another system can start work here. Add it to `kortix.yaml`, tell me the URL and which secret holds the signing key, and write the prompt it fires.

connector-setup.label: Connect a tool I use
connector-setup.prompt: Tell me which connector is worth setting up first for a company like mine, what it would let you actually do once it is connected, and what you would need me to approve.

memory-curate.label: Tidy up project memory
memory-curate.prompt: Read project memory, find what is stale, duplicated or vague, and rewrite it so a fresh session gets the truth in one pass. Open a change request with the diff.

memory-gaps.label: Find your blind spots
memory-gaps.prompt: Look at project memory and tell me the ten things you would need to know to do my job well but currently do not. Ask them as one numbered list I can answer in a single reply.

harness-improve.label: Improve yourself
harness-improve.prompt: Look at what recent sessions in this project actually did, find where you got stuck or repeated work, and refine the prompts, skills and memory that caused it. Open one change request titled `harness: …`.

cr-open.label: Open your first change request
cr-open.prompt: Pick the most useful improvement you can make to this project right now, make it, and open a change request explaining what you changed and why. Keep it small enough that I can review it in two minutes.

repo-tour.label: Explain my own repo to me
repo-tour.prompt: Walk me through this project as it stands — what is configured, which agents exist, what is connected, what is empty — and tell me the three things worth setting up next.

agent-onboarder.label: Make an onboarding agent
agent-onboarder.prompt: Create an agent whose job is onboarding new people at my company: it answers their questions from memory, points them at the right docs, and flags what it could not answer. Open a change request.

agent-watcher.label: Make a competitor watcher
agent-watcher.prompt: Create an agent plus a weekly trigger that watches our competitors and tells me only what actually changed. Add both to the repo disabled, and show me a sample of this week's output.

agent-inbox.label: Make an inbox triager
agent-inbox.prompt: Create an agent that triages an inbox — sorts what needs me, what needs a reply, and what can wait — and writes a short summary. Open a change request with the agent and its grants.

csv-dashboard.label: Turn a CSV into a dashboard
csv-dashboard.prompt: I am attaching a raw CSV. Build me a real dashboard from it — the charts that actually explain the data, on a page I can open — and send me the URL. If nothing is attached, tell me in one line instead of waiting.

csv-charts.label: Chart this CSV properly
csv-charts.prompt: I am attaching a CSV. Pick the right chart for each question the data answers, build them, and caption each one with what it shows. No pie charts unless a pie chart is genuinely right.

spreadsheet-analysis.label: Make sense of a spreadsheet
spreadsheet-analysis.prompt: Read the spreadsheet I have attached, find the patterns and the outliers, and write me a short summary of what I should actually do about them. If nothing is attached, tell me in one line instead of waiting.

metrics-dashboard.label: Build a metrics dashboard
metrics-dashboard.prompt: Build me a live dashboard of the numbers a company like mine watches weekly, as a working web app, and send me the URL. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

kpi-wall.label: Build a KPI wall
kpi-wall.prompt: Build me a single page that shows whether the company is on track — the five numbers that matter, each with its target and its trend. Working web app, send me the URL.

sheet-to-app.label: Turn a sheet into an app
sheet-to-app.prompt: I am attaching a spreadsheet my team edits by hand. Turn it into a proper web app with a form and a table so nobody breaks it again, and send me the URL.

crm-lite.label: Build a lightweight CRM
crm-lite.prompt: Build me a lightweight CRM as a working web app — companies, contacts, deal stage, next action — seeded with a few realistic rows so I can see it working. Send me the URL.

task-board.label: Build a task board
task-board.prompt: Build me a task board as a working web app — columns, drag between them, and it remembers what I did. Send me the URL.

intake-form.label: Build an intake form
intake-form.prompt: Build me an intake form as a working web app — the questions a new client should answer before a first call — with the answers saved where I can read them. Send me the URL.

pricing-calculator.label: Build a pricing calculator
pricing-calculator.prompt: Build me a pricing calculator as a working web app so a prospect can estimate what they would pay, and send me the URL. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

feedback-board.label: Build a feedback board
feedback-board.prompt: Build me a customer feedback board as a working web app — submit an idea, upvote, a status on each — and send me the URL.

inventory-tracker.label: Build an inventory tracker
inventory-tracker.prompt: Build me an inventory tracker as a working web app — items, counts, low-stock warnings — and send me the URL.

status-page.label: Build a status page
status-page.prompt: Build me a status page as a working web app — components, current state, an incident history — and send me the URL.

clean-data.label: Clean up my data
clean-data.prompt: I am attaching a messy spreadsheet. Clean it — consistent columns, fixed dates, trimmed text, no duplicates — and give me a change log of everything you altered.

runway.label: Work out my runway
runway.prompt: I am attaching our numbers. Work out our burn rate and how many months of runway we have, show the working so I can argue with it, and tell me the two levers that move it most.

budget-variance.label: Compare budget to actual
budget-variance.prompt: I am attaching our budget and our actuals. Show me where we are over and under, rank the gaps by size, and tell me which ones are worth acting on.

cashflow-forecast.label: Forecast our cash
cashflow-forecast.prompt: I am attaching our transactions. Build a cash-flow forecast for the next six months, be explicit about what it assumes, and flag the month we get tight.

unit-economics.label: Work out unit economics
unit-economics.prompt: Work out what one customer actually costs us and what they are worth — acquisition, delivery, support, retention — and tell me which number to fix first. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

pricing-model.label: Model a price change
pricing-model.prompt: Model what happens if we change our pricing — the packaging, the per-seat maths, and the revenue effect at three adoption levels. Give me the spreadsheet and a one-paragraph recommendation.

invoice-reconcile.label: Reconcile my invoices
invoice-reconcile.prompt: I am attaching invoices and a bank export. Match them up, list what is unmatched in both directions, and tell me what looks like a duplicate charge.

expense-categorise.label: Categorise our spend
expense-categorise.prompt: I am attaching our expenses. Categorise them, break the spend down by category and by month, find what is growing fastest, and name the three I should cut first.

subscription-audit.label: Find wasted spend
subscription-audit.prompt: I am attaching our card statements. Find every recurring charge, flag the ones that look unused or duplicated, and total what cancelling them would save per year.

ar-chase.label: Chase unpaid invoices
ar-chase.prompt: I am attaching our receivables. Work out who owes what and how late, then draft the chase email for each one — firm, not rude — ordered by how much is at stake.

financial-model.label: Build a financial model
financial-model.prompt: Build me a simple financial model — revenue, costs, cash, runway — driven off an assumptions tab I can change, with a chart of cash over time. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

cohort-revenue.label: Analyse revenue cohorts
cohort-revenue.prompt: I am attaching customer revenue data. Build a cohort analysis, tell me in one paragraph whether retention is improving, and show which cohort changed.

headcount-cost.label: Plan hiring costs
headcount-cost.prompt: Build me a hiring plan as a spreadsheet — role, when, fully loaded cost, and what it unlocks — totalled by month against our runway.

margin-analysis.label: Find my best margins
margin-analysis.prompt: I am attaching sales data. Work out margin by product, customer and channel, and tell me what we should be selling more of and what is quietly losing money.

board-metrics.label: Build the board metrics pack
board-metrics.prompt: Build the numbers pack a board expects — growth, burn, runway, retention, pipeline — as charts with a one-line read on each. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

pitch-deck.label: Build a deck
pitch-deck.prompt: Build me a 10-slide deck introducing my company: what we do, who it is for, the problem, how it works, and why now. Write the words and design the slides — do not hand me an outline. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

deck-from-doc.label: Turn a doc into a deck
deck-from-doc.prompt: I am attaching a document. Turn it into a deck that stands up in a meeting — one idea per slide, speaker notes underneath — rather than pasting the paragraphs onto slides.

investor-update.label: Build an investor update
investor-update.prompt: Build me this month's investor update — highlights, metrics, lowlights, and what I need help with. Pull the numbers rather than asking me for them. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

board-deck.label: Build a board deck
board-deck.prompt: Build me a board deck — where we are against plan, the three decisions I need from the board, and the risks I am not going to hide. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

sales-deck.label: Build a sales deck
sales-deck.prompt: Build me a sales deck for a first call — their problem, our answer, proof, and the next step — with speaker notes. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

data-slide.label: Turn numbers into slides
data-slide.prompt: I am attaching data. Build the three slides that tell its story — one chart each, one sentence of takeaway each — ready to present.

pdf-report.label: Make a proper PDF report
pdf-report.prompt: Take what we have been working on and lay it out as a real PDF report — cover, contents, page numbers, charts — that I can send to a client without editing it.

proposal.label: Write a proposal
proposal.prompt: Write a client proposal — the problem as they described it, what we would do, the plan, and the price with the number left as a placeholder. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

one-pager.label: Write a one-pager
one-pager.prompt: Write a one-pager on my company I can send before a meeting — what we do, who for, why it matters, what to do next. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

contract-explain.label: Explain a contract
contract-explain.prompt: I am attaching a contract. Explain it in plain language — the obligations, the money, the termination terms, the dates — then list the questions I should take to a lawyer. Do not tell me whether to sign.

meeting-actions.label: Turn notes into actions
meeting-actions.prompt: I am pasting my meeting notes next. Turn them into decisions, owners and dates, and tell me plainly what was left unresolved.

weekly-report.label: Write the weekly report
weekly-report.prompt: Write this week's company report — what moved, what did not, and what I should worry about — pulling from the repo and memory rather than asking me.

case-study.label: Write a case study
case-study.prompt: Write a customer case study — the situation, what changed, the result — using a codename if I have not given you a real customer. Publish it as a page and send me the URL.

hard-email.label: Write the hard email
hard-email.prompt: Help me write the email I have been putting off — a price rise, a delay, or bad news. Ask which one in a single line, then give me three versions from blunt to gentle.

competitor-teardown.label: Tear down a competitor
competitor-teardown.prompt: Pick our closest competitor and take them apart: positioning, pricing, what they ship, what customers praise and complain about, and the two places we can beat them. Cite every source.

pricing-benchmark.label: Benchmark our pricing
pricing-benchmark.prompt: Research what comparable products charge, put it in one table with the packaging and the per-seat maths, and tell me where we sit and whether that is deliberate.

lead-list.label: Build me a lead list
lead-list.prompt: Build a list of 25 companies that fit our customer profile, with why each fits and the best person to reach. Spreadsheet, with sources.

investor-list.label: Build an investor list
investor-list.prompt: Build a list of investors who back companies like mine at our stage — fund, partner, a recent relevant cheque, and the warmest path in. Spreadsheet, with sources.

market-sizing.label: Size my market
market-sizing.prompt: Size the market I am selling into, top down and bottom up, and show the working and the sources so I can argue with the numbers.

review-mining.label: Mine competitor reviews
review-mining.prompt: Read the public reviews of our competitors, pull out what people repeatedly praise and complain about, and turn it into the three things we should say on our site.

industry-catchup.label: Catch me up on my industry
industry-catchup.prompt: Catch me up on my industry over the last month — what shipped, who raised, what changed — then tell me which two items actually matter to us and why.

keyword-research.label: Find what buyers search
keyword-research.prompt: Research what our buyers actually search for, group it by intent, and tell me the five pages worth writing first. Spreadsheet, with sources.

buyer-research.label: Research my buyers
buyer-research.prompt: Research the people who buy products like mine — where they gather, what they complain about, and the words they use for the problem. Cite sources.

regulation-scan.label: Scan the rules that apply
regulation-scan.prompt: Research the rules and standards that apply to a company like mine, summarise what each asks for in plain language, and flag what I should take to a lawyer rather than act on.

events-list.label: Find events worth attending
events-list.prompt: Find the conferences and meetups where our buyers actually are this year — date, place, cost, and whether it is worth it. Spreadsheet.

landing-page.label: Ship a landing page
landing-page.prompt: Build a landing page for my product and publish it. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me. Send me the live URL when it is up.

pricing-page.label: Ship a pricing page
pricing-page.prompt: Write and publish a pricing page — the tiers, what is in each, and the objections the page has to answer. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

docs-site.label: Publish a docs site
docs-site.prompt: Build and publish a small docs site for my product — getting started, the core concepts, and one how-to. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

changelog-page.label: Publish a changelog
changelog-page.prompt: Build and publish a changelog page, and write the recent entries from the history in this repo rather than asking me what shipped.

comparison-page.label: Ship a comparison page
comparison-page.prompt: Build and publish an honest comparison between us and our closest alternative — where each one wins. Research the other side rather than inventing it.

seo-pass.label: Do an SEO pass
seo-pass.prompt: Audit my site for SEO — titles, descriptions, headings, alt text, internal links, sitemap — fix what you can, and list what needs a decision from me.

homepage-rewrite.label: Rewrite my homepage
homepage-rewrite.prompt: Rewrite my homepage so the first screen says what we do, who it is for, and what to do next. Publish it and show me the before and after side by side.

waitlist-page.label: Put up a waitlist page
waitlist-page.prompt: Build and publish a waitlist page for something I am about to launch — a headline, the promise, one email capture. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

blog-post.label: Write and publish a post
blog-post.prompt: Write a post about something my company actually knows, publish it to our site, and send me the URL. Pick the topic that would be most useful to our buyers and say why.

faq-page.label: Write an FAQ page
faq-page.prompt: Write and publish an FAQ answering the ten questions a first-time buyer actually asks. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

careers-page.label: Put up a careers page
careers-page.prompt: Build and publish a careers page — how we work, what we are hiring for, how to apply. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

storefront-copy.label: Write our listing copy
storefront-copy.prompt: Write our listing copy for a marketplace or app store — the title, the short pitch, the long description, and the screenshots I should take.

cold-email.label: Write a cold email sequence
cold-email.prompt: Write a four-email cold sequence to our ideal customer — short, specific, no flattery — and say what each one is meant to do.

launch-announcement.label: Write a launch announcement
launch-announcement.prompt: Write the launch announcement for our next release in three lengths — a post, an email, and one line — all saying the same thing.

newsletter.label: Draft the newsletter
newsletter.prompt: Draft this month's customer newsletter — what shipped, what we learned, and one useful thing they can act on.

social-calendar.label: Plan a content calendar
social-calendar.prompt: Plan a month of content — theme, piece, channel, date — as a spreadsheet I can hand to someone.

linkedin-posts.label: Write a week of posts
linkedin-posts.prompt: Write a week of posts about what we are building — one idea each, written like a person, no engagement bait.

positioning.label: Sharpen our positioning
positioning.prompt: Write our positioning: the category, who it is for, the alternative, and the one thing we do better. Give me three options, recommend one, and say why.

icp-definition.label: Define our ideal customer
icp-definition.prompt: Write down who we are actually for — the company, the person, the trigger that makes them look — and who we should say no to.

objection-handling.label: Answer our objections
objection-handling.prompt: List the objections we get in sales and write the honest answer to each — not a deflection.

win-loss.label: Analyse wins and losses
win-loss.prompt: I am attaching our recent deals. Find the patterns in what we win and lose, and tell me the one change that would move the rate most.

interview-guide.label: Write customer questions
interview-guide.prompt: Write the questions for a customer interview that would actually teach us something — open, not leading — plus what I am listening for in each answer.

referral-program.label: Design a referral program
referral-program.prompt: Design a referral program for my product — the incentive, the mechanics, the wording — and tell me how it could be abused.

brand-voice.label: Write our voice guide
brand-voice.prompt: Write our brand voice guide — how we sound, how we do not — with before-and-after rewrites of real copy from our site.

code-review.label: Review my code
code-review.prompt: Review the code in this repo the way a senior engineer would — correctness first, then clarity. Give me a prioritised list, worst first, and open a change request for the fixes you are confident about.

write-tests.label: Write the missing tests
write-tests.prompt: Find the code in this repo that would hurt most if it broke and has no test, write the tests, and open a change request. Tell me what you deliberately did not cover and why.

fix-bug.label: Fix a bug I describe
fix-bug.prompt: I am going to describe a bug. Reproduce it in this repo first, then fix the cause rather than the symptom, add a test that would have caught it, and open a change request.

explain-codebase.label: Explain this codebase
explain-codebase.prompt: Walk me through this codebase — what it does, how it is laid out, where the important logic lives, and the three things that would confuse a new engineer.

refactor-file.label: Clean up a messy file
refactor-file.prompt: Find the file in this repo that is doing too much, split it along its real seams without changing behaviour, and open a change request. Prove behaviour is unchanged with the tests.

deps-upgrade.label: Upgrade my dependencies
deps-upgrade.prompt: Check this repo's dependencies for outdated and vulnerable versions, upgrade what is safe, run the tests, and open a change request listing anything that needs a human decision.

readme.label: Write the README
readme.prompt: Write the README this repo should have — what it is, how to run it, how to work on it — from the code rather than from guesses. Open a change request.

ci-setup.label: Set up CI
ci-setup.prompt: Set up continuous integration for this repo — install, typecheck, lint, test — so a change request tells me whether it is safe before I read it. Open it as a change request.

api-client.label: Write an API client
api-client.prompt: Write a typed client for an API I need to call, with the error handling and retries already in it, plus a test against a recorded response. Ask which API in one line.

security-review.label: Review my code for risks
security-review.prompt: Review this repo for the security mistakes that actually happen — secrets in source, unvalidated input, missing authorisation checks — and open a change request for what you can fix safely.

perf-audit.label: Find what is slow
perf-audit.prompt: Find the slowest paths in this project, measure rather than guess, and tell me the one change that would help most. Show me the numbers before and after.

error-handling.label: Add proper error handling
error-handling.prompt: Find where this code fails silently or throws something a person cannot act on, fix it so every failure says what happened and what to do, and open a change request.

db-migration.label: Write a database migration
db-migration.prompt: Write the migration I need against this project's schema, with the rollback, and tell me what would happen to existing rows. Open a change request rather than running it.

api-docs.label: Document my API
api-docs.prompt: Document this project's API from the code — every route, its inputs, its responses, its errors — and publish it as a page I can send to someone.

dead-code.label: Find dead code
dead-code.prompt: Find the code in this repo nothing reaches any more, prove it with the import graph rather than by eye, and open a change request that deletes it.

branch-explain.label: Explain what changed
branch-explain.prompt: Read the recent history of this repo and tell me what actually changed and why, in the order that makes sense to a person who was away.

api-to-sheet.label: Pull an API into a sheet
api-to-sheet.prompt: Pull the data I need out of an API and keep it in a spreadsheet I can actually read. Ask which API in one line, then build it and show me the first pull.

recurring-export.label: Set up a recurring export
recurring-export.prompt: Set up an export that runs on a schedule and drops the data where I need it, as a trigger in `kortix.yaml`. Show me one run's output before you leave it enabled.

page-monitor.label: Watch a page for changes
page-monitor.prompt: Watch a page that matters to me and tell me only when something meaningful changes — not every whitespace edit. Set it up as a scheduled trigger and show me today's diff.

scraper.label: Build me a scraper
scraper.prompt: Build a scraper for a site I name, put the results somewhere I can query, and be explicit about what it will do when the page structure changes.

reconcile-systems.label: Reconcile two systems
reconcile-systems.prompt: I am attaching exports from two systems that should agree. Find every row where they do not, tell me which side looks wrong, and give me the list to fix.

alert-threshold.label: Alert me when a number moves
alert-threshold.prompt: Set up a check that watches a number I care about and tells me when it crosses a line I set — not a daily report I will stop reading. Add it as a trigger.

form-to-sheet.label: Pipe form replies into a sheet
form-to-sheet.prompt: Take the replies from a form we already use and get them into a spreadsheet automatically, deduplicated and typed properly.

digest-sources.label: Digest my sources daily
digest-sources.prompt: Pick the handful of sources I actually need to follow, and set up a daily trigger that reads them and sends me only what changed and why it matters.

job-description.label: Write a job description
job-description.prompt: Write the job description for the role I most need to fill — what they will actually do in the first 90 days, not a wishlist of skills. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

cv-screen.label: Screen CVs for me
cv-screen.prompt: I am attaching CVs and the role. Score each against what the job actually needs, rank them, and tell me plainly which two I should talk to and why.

interview-plan.label: Plan an interview loop
interview-plan.prompt: Design the interview loop for a role — who asks what, in what order, and what each stage is trying to find out. Include the questions.

role-scorecard.label: Write a role scorecard
role-scorecard.prompt: Write a scorecard for a role — the outcomes it owns, how we would know it is going well, and what failure looks like at 90 days. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

onboarding-plan.label: Write a 30-60-90 plan
onboarding-plan.prompt: Write a 30-60-90 day plan for someone joining my company — what they read, who they meet, and what they own by the end of each stage. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

team-handbook.label: Write our team handbook
team-handbook.prompt: Write the handbook a new person reads in week one — how we work, where things live, who to ask, what good looks like — from what is already in this repo and memory.

reference-questions.label: Write reference questions
reference-questions.prompt: Write the reference-check questions that would actually tell me something — specific, hard to answer with a platitude — plus what a bad answer sounds like.

comp-bands.label: Draft compensation bands
comp-bands.prompt: Research what people in our roles are paid in our market and draft honest salary bands with the reasoning. Cite your sources.

review-template.label: Write a review template
review-template.prompt: Write the performance review template for my company — short, specific, about outcomes rather than personality — plus how to run the conversation.

offer-letter.label: Draft an offer letter
offer-letter.prompt: Draft an offer letter for a role, leaving the numbers as placeholders, and flag which clauses a lawyer should look at rather than deciding them yourself.

help-centre.label: Build a help centre
help-centre.prompt: Build and publish a help centre for my product — the articles people actually need, written from what is in this repo — and send me the URL.

canned-replies.label: Write our canned replies
canned-replies.prompt: Write the saved replies for the questions we answer over and over — helpful, human, and short enough that someone will actually use them.

support-triage.label: Triage my support backlog
support-triage.prompt: I am attaching our open tickets. Sort them into what needs me, what needs a reply, and what can be closed, and draft the replies for the second group.

incident-note.label: Write a customer incident note
incident-note.prompt: Something broke and I need to tell customers. Write the note — what happened, who it affected, what we are doing — honest, no hedging, no blame-shifting.

faq-from-tickets.label: Turn tickets into an FAQ
faq-from-tickets.prompt: I am attaching our support tickets. Find the questions that keep coming back, write the answers once, and publish them as an FAQ page.

churn-analysis.label: Work out why people leave
churn-analysis.prompt: I am attaching our churn data and any cancellation reasons. Find the real patterns, separate them from the noise, and tell me the one thing worth fixing first.

nps-analysis.label: Read our customer feedback
nps-analysis.prompt: I am attaching customer feedback. Group it by theme, tell me what people love and what they keep asking for, and quote the lines worth putting on the wall.

onboarding-emails.label: Write onboarding emails
onboarding-emails.prompt: Write the emails a new customer gets in their first two weeks — each one earning its place by teaching something, not by checking in. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

refund-policy.label: Draft a refund policy
refund-policy.prompt: Draft a refund policy that is fair and unambiguous, publish it, and flag anything a lawyer should review before it goes live.

vendor-list.label: List our vendors and renewals
vendor-list.prompt: Work out every tool and vendor we pay for, what each costs, and when it renews. Put it in a spreadsheet and flag the renewals in the next 60 days.

meeting-agenda.label: Write the meeting agenda
meeting-agenda.prompt: Write the agenda for a meeting I have coming up — the decisions to make, the material to read first, and a time budget per item.

ops-review.label: Run my weekly review
ops-review.prompt: Run my weekly review: pull what changed in this repo and in memory, tell me what moved, what slipped, and the three things worth my attention on Monday.

process-map.label: Map how our work flows
process-map.prompt: Map how work actually flows through my company from request to delivered, name where it gets stuck, and propose the one change that would help most. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

okr-draft.label: Draft this quarter goals
okr-draft.prompt: Draft this quarter's goals — three objectives, measurable results under each, and what we are explicitly not doing. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

decision-log.label: Start a decision log
decision-log.prompt: Read this repo's history and memory, reconstruct the decisions that were actually made and why, and write them into a decision log I can keep adding to.

risk-register.label: Build a risk register
risk-register.prompt: List what could realistically go wrong for a company like mine, rank by likelihood and damage, and name the cheapest thing that reduces each. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

asset-inventory.label: Inventory our accounts
asset-inventory.prompt: Work out every account, domain and service this company depends on, who controls each, and what breaks if we lose access. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

sop-library.label: Build our SOP library
sop-library.prompt: Turn the things my company does repeatedly into written procedures, organised so someone can find the right one in ten seconds. Start with the three highest-value ones.

calendar-audit.label: Audit where my time goes
calendar-audit.prompt: I am attaching my calendar export. Tell me where my time actually goes, which meetings have no clear output, and what I should cut or shorten.

north-star.label: Define our north-star metric
north-star.prompt: Work out the one number that best tells us whether this company is working, argue for it against the two runners-up, and say how we would measure it. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

tracking-plan.label: Write an event tracking plan
tracking-plan.prompt: Write the event tracking plan for my product — the events worth capturing, their properties, and the questions each one answers. Skip the ones nobody will query.

ab-test-design.label: Design an A/B test
ab-test-design.prompt: Design an experiment for a change I am considering — the hypothesis, the metric, the sample size, and how long it has to run to mean anything.

experiment-analysis.label: Analyse an experiment
experiment-analysis.prompt: I am attaching experiment results. Tell me whether the difference is real, what it would be worth if we shipped it, and be honest if the answer is inconclusive.

funnel-analysis.label: Find where the funnel leaks
funnel-analysis.prompt: I am attaching funnel data. Find the step where we lose the most people, quantify what fixing it is worth, and suggest what to try.

retention-curve.label: Chart our retention
retention-curve.prompt: I am attaching usage data. Chart retention over time, tell me whether the curve flattens, and what that says about whether we have found product-market fit.

segment-analysis.label: Find our best customers
segment-analysis.prompt: I am attaching customer data. Work out which segment retains and pays best, and tell me what they have in common that we could target deliberately.

dashboard-spec.label: Decide what to measure
dashboard-spec.prompt: Tell me which numbers this company should actually watch weekly and which are vanity, then build the dashboard for the survivors.

brand-palette.label: Pick a brand palette
brand-palette.prompt: Put together a brand palette and type scale for my company — the colours, where each is used, and the contrast ratios — as a one-page reference I can hand to anyone.

design-review.label: Review my design
design-review.prompt: Look at my site or product and review the design — hierarchy, spacing, type, colour, contrast. Give me a prioritised list, worst first, with what to change.

logo-brief.label: Write a logo brief
logo-brief.prompt: Write the brief I would hand a designer for our logo — what the company is, the feeling, what to avoid, and three directions worth exploring. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

slide-template.label: Design a slide template
slide-template.prompt: Design a reusable slide template for my company — title, section, content, metric and quote layouts — and save it so future decks start from it.

social-templates.label: Design social templates
social-templates.prompt: Design the image templates we reuse for social posts, in our own colours and type, and save them so they are one edit away from ready.

email-template.label: Design an email template
email-template.prompt: Design the HTML email template we send from — readable on a phone, degrades gracefully, no images required to make sense — and save it in the repo.

ui-audit.label: Audit our UI consistency
ui-audit.prompt: Go through our product and find where the same thing looks different in two places — buttons, spacing, wording, states — and list the fixes worst first.

icon-set.label: Pick an icon set
icon-set.prompt: Pick an icon set that fits our brand, explain why it fits, and show it applied to the ten places we most use icons.

privacy-policy.label: Draft a privacy policy
privacy-policy.prompt: Draft a privacy policy that describes what we actually do with data rather than boilerplate, and list every claim a lawyer needs to confirm before it goes live.

terms-of-service.label: Draft terms of service
terms-of-service.prompt: Draft terms of service for my product in plain language, and flag every clause that needs a lawyer rather than deciding it yourself.

security-questionnaire.label: Answer a security questionnaire
security-questionnaire.prompt: I am attaching a security questionnaire from a customer. Draft honest answers from what is actually true of this project, and mark clearly every one I have to verify myself.

dpa-checklist.label: Check our data agreements
dpa-checklist.prompt: List the data-processing agreements a company like mine typically needs, what each one covers, and which ones we appear to be missing. Flag what to take to a lawyer.

sow-draft.label: Draft a scope of work
sow-draft.prompt: Draft a scope of work — deliverables, milestones, what is out of scope, and what I need from the client. Flag anything a lawyer should look at. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.

nda-explain.label: Explain an NDA
nda-explain.prompt: I am attaching an NDA. Tell me in plain language what I would be agreeing to, what is unusual about it, and the questions to ask before signing. Do not tell me whether to sign.

plan-week.label: Plan my week
plan-week.prompt: Look at what is actually going on in this project and plan my week — what matters, what can wait, and what I should say no to. Be opinionated.

meeting-prep.label: Prep me for a meeting
meeting-prep.prompt: I have a meeting coming up. Research who I am meeting, pull what we already know about them from memory, and give me a one-page brief with the three questions to ask.

catch-up.label: Tell me what I missed
catch-up.prompt: I have been away. Tell me what happened in this project while I was gone, what needs a decision from me, and what is on fire — in that order.

draft-replies.label: Draft my replies
draft-replies.prompt: I am attaching messages I owe replies to. Draft each one in my voice, shortest acceptable version first, and flag the two I should handle personally.

summarise-thread.label: Summarise a long thread
summarise-thread.prompt: I am attaching a long thread. Tell me what was actually agreed, what is still open, and what I owe someone — and skip the small talk.

daily-standup.label: Write my standup
daily-standup.prompt: Read what actually changed in this project since yesterday and write my standup from the evidence — done, doing, blocked — rather than asking me.

follow-ups.label: Chase my follow-ups
follow-ups.prompt: Go through recent sessions and memory, find everything I said I would do and have not, and give me the list in the order I should clear it.

reading-digest.label: Digest what I saved
reading-digest.prompt: I am attaching links and documents I saved and never read. Read them for me, tell me which two were worth it, and summarise those properly.

explain-concept.label: Explain this to my team
explain-concept.prompt: Explain something technical to my team in language they will actually follow — no jargon, one worked example, and the two things people usually get wrong. Ask me the topic in one line.

training-course.label: Build a training course
training-course.prompt: Build a short course that teaches someone to do one job at my company end to end — the lessons, the exercises, and how they know they have got it. Pick the job that would help most.

glossary.label: Write our glossary
glossary.prompt: Write the glossary of terms my company uses — including the ones we use differently from everyone else — from what is already in this repo and memory.

how-to-guide.label: Write a how-to guide
how-to-guide.prompt: Write the how-to guide for the thing people keep asking me to explain, with screenshots or commands where they help. Publish it and send me the URL.

runbook.label: Write a runbook
runbook.prompt: Write a runbook for a job my company does over and over, step by step, so someone else could run it without asking me. Pick the highest-value one and say why.

onboarding-doc.label: Write the onboarding doc
onboarding-doc.prompt: Write the document a new hire reads in their first week — how we work, where things live, who to ask, what good looks like. Take what you can from project memory, and list anything you had to guess at the end rather than stopping to ask me.
